# Foundations of machine learning {.unnumbered}

> *"All models are wrong but some are useful."* — George E. P. Box
> [@box1979].

This part corresponds to the third course of the master: the foundations of
machine learning. It takes a reader who can program in Python (Part I) to the
point of turning a table of data into a predictive or descriptive model —
and, above all, of **judging how far that model can be trusted**. The thread
running through every chapter is the one that separates machine learning from
curve fitting: a model is built on some data and must be judged on other data.

The chapters follow the workflow of a project: what learning from data means
and which families of methods exist; how data arrive — in which formats, with
which types of variables — and how they become a table; how to prepare the
features without compromising the evaluation; linear regression for numerical
targets; overfitting, validation and regularisation; classification and its
metrics; and clustering, for data without labels.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this part matters for an AI engineer
Every system an AI engineer builds — from a price estimator to a large
language model — is fitted on data and judged on other data. The vocabulary
and the tools of this part (losses and risks, train/validation/test splits,
cross-validation, the bias–variance trade-off, regularisation, metrics that
reflect the cost of errors, pipelines that prevent leakage) are the ones used,
unchanged, by deep learning and by the evaluation of generative models. The
simple models studied here are also the **baselines** against which every
complex model must be compared.
:::

## What you will be able to do {.unnumbered}

1. Define machine learning precisely, distinguish its paradigms, and prove
   which predictor is optimal for squared and 0–1 losses; explain why the
   training error is optimistic and how large a test set must be
   (@sec-ch-ml-intro).
2. Build an analysis-ready table from CSV, JSON, XML, HTML and Excel files,
   classify variables by type and describe their distributions
   (@sec-ch-ml-data).
3. Encode categorical variables, scale numerical ones, handle missing values,
   and keep every learned step inside a pipeline to prevent data leakage
   (@sec-ch-ml-preprocessing).
4. Fit and interpret simple, multiple and polynomial linear regressions,
   derive least squares and its properties, and evaluate them with MSE, RMSE,
   MAE and $R^2$ (@sec-ch-ml-regression).
5. Diagnose overfitting with the bias–variance decomposition, learning curves,
   hold-out and cross-validation, and control it with ridge, lasso and elastic
   net (@sec-ch-ml-regularization).
6. Build binary and multiclass classifiers with logistic regression, and
   evaluate them with confusion matrices, precision, recall, $F_1$, ROC curves
   and cost-based thresholds (@sec-ch-ml-classification).
7. Find groups in unlabelled data with k-means, evaluate them and choose their
   number (@sec-ch-ml-clustering).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

Part I, in particular @sec-ch-functions and @sec-ch-oop (functions and
classes), @sec-ch-files (CSV and JSON files) and the crash course on NumPy,
pandas and Matplotlib (@sec-crash-courses), whose matrix product and
variance identities are used throughout. The mathematics — derivatives,
vectors and matrices, means and variances — is introduced or recalled where it
is needed; proofs that use more are in the deep dives.

## Libraries and data used {.unnumbered}

The code of this part was executed with **Python 3.13.18**, **scikit-learn 1.9.1** [@pedregosa2011], **NumPy 2.5.3**, **pandas 3.0.5** and **Matplotlib 3.11.2**; every output shown was produced by actually running it when the book was built.


The models use the scikit-learn interface (`fit`, `predict`, `transform`,
pipelines), introduced in @sec-ml-workflow. A small helper module,
[`ml/mlbook.py`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-engineering-handbook/blob/main/ml/mlbook.py),
fixes the figure style and loads the house-sales data.

The data are either generated in the code (so that the truth is known and the
methods can be checked against it) or public data sets with a clear licence:
the house sales of the project — a CC0 copy of a sample of 1987 sales in
Windsor, Canada, whose provenance is verified in @sec-housing-data
[@yasser2021; @anglin1996] — and two classic data sets that ship with
scikit-learn, the Wisconsin diagnostic breast-cancer data [@wolberg1993] and
the wine data [@aeberhard1992], both under CC BY 4.0.

## Map of the part {.unnumbered}

| Chapter | Core topics | What the book adds |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-ch-ml-intro | what machine learning is, why now, families of techniques | risk and empirical risk, optimality of the conditional mean and of the Bayes classifier, optimism of the training error, Chebyshev and Hoeffding bounds for test sets, memorising vs learning, no free lunch, the scikit-learn API |
| @sec-ch-ml-data | structured and unstructured data, variable types, reading CSV/TSV, JSON, XML, HTML, Excel | tidy data, Stevens' levels of measurement and which summaries are meaningful (proved), skewness and its invariance, dialects and encodings of CSV, a first-look routine |
| @sec-ch-ml-preprocessing | encoding, scaling, missing data | the dummy-variable trap, equivariance of least squares under rescaling vs penalised models, MCAR/MAR/MNAR, what mean imputation does to the variance, leakage demonstrated on pure noise, pipelines |
| @sec-ch-ml-regression | simple and multiple linear regression, least squares, cost functions, $R^2$, correlation matrix, polynomial regression | least squares as maximum likelihood, gradient descent and its rate, normal equations, $R^2$ decomposition, Cauchy–Schwarz, Frisch–Waugh–Lovell, VIF, Gauss–Markov |
| @sec-ch-ml-regularization | bias–variance, overfitting, hold-out, k-fold and leave-one-out CV, ridge, lasso, elastic net, learning curves | the decomposition proved and simulated, the LOOCV shortcut, nested CV, ridge shrinkage and Hoerl–Kennard, soft thresholding, $\lambda_{\max}$, coordinate descent, scikit-learn's penalty scalings |
| @sec-ch-ml-classification | binary and multiclass classification, logistic regression, metrics, decision boundary, ROC | cross-entropy gradient and convexity, separability, softmax gradient, $F_1$ bounds, the cost-optimal threshold, AUC as a ranking probability |
| @sec-ch-ml-clustering | clustering vs classification, k-means, metrics, number of clusters, elbow method | the mean as optimal centre, convergence of Lloyd's algorithm, k-means++, silhouette range, why inertia cannot choose $k$, scaling and failure cases |
| @sec-ch-project-housing | the final project | requirements, data provenance, a forensic re-execution and code review of the published notebook, a reference implementation with nested cross-validation |

## The final project {.unnumbered}

The course ends with a comparison of **regularised regression models for
estimating house prices**: starting from a data set of residential sales, the
analysis must explore and prepare the data with motivated choices, fit an
unregularised baseline, compare ridge, lasso and elastic net with
cross-validation, read their coefficients and residuals, and close with a
recommendation that people who do not write code can follow.
@sec-ch-project-housing states the requirements in my own words, verifies
where the data come from, maps each requirement to the chapters above, reviews
the notebook I submitted — re-executing it to explain every number it prints —
and presents a reference implementation that applies the review's
suggestions.
